Danish

Etymology 1

From Old Danish iak, iæk, iægh, æk, ak, from Old Norse ek, Old East Norse iak, from Proto-Germanic *ek, *ik (“I”), from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm, *eǵh₂óm.

Alternative forms

  • a, æ, ja, jæ (dialectal)

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): [jɑ̈(j)]
  • Rhymes: -aj

Pronoun

jeg (accusative mig, possessive min)

  1. (personal) I
Usage notes

Frequently omitted in informal, written contexts, such as text messaging, memoranda and profiles.

Norwegian Bokmål

Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
Jeg (filosofi)
Wikipedia no

Etymology 1

Ultimately inherited from Old Norse ek (“I”), from Proto-Norse ᛖᚲ (ek), beside ᛖᚲᚨ (eka), from Proto-Germanic *ek, earlier *eka, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm (“I”). Forms with initial j-, including jek and jeg, are attested in Middle Norwegian; their spread has been attributed to East Scandinavian, particularly Swedish, influence.[1] Doublet of ego.

Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk eg, Danish jeg, Swedish jag, Icelandic ég, German ich, Latin ego and English I (“I”).

Pronunciation

  • (stressed) IPA(key): /jæɪ̯/, [jæɪ̯]
  • (unstressed) IPA(key): /jæ/, [jæ]
  • Audio:(file)
  • Rhymes: -æɪ̯
  • Homophone: jei
  • Hyphenation: jeg

Pronoun

jeg (objective meg, possessive min or mi or mitt or mine, plural vi)

  1. I; the first-person singular personal pronoun, used by a speaker or writer to refer to themselves.
    Jeg kommer tilbake i morgen. ― I will return tomorrow.
    Det var jeg som ringte. ― It was I who called.
    • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, 3rd edition, page 38:
      Jeg heder Solvejg. – Og hvad heder du?
      I am called Solveig. And what are you called?
    • 1896, Henrik Ibsen, John Gabriel Borkman‎, page 164:
      Men ingen af alle de andre hørte det. Bare jeg alene.
      But none of the others heard it. Only I did.
    • 1907, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Ørneredet”, in Bjørnstjerne Bjørnsons Fortællinger‎, page 193:
      jeg, jeg holder af dig, og deroppe har du intet at vinde!
      I, I love you, and you have nothing to gain up there!
    • 1915, Barbra Ring, Før kulden kommer, page 36:
      stakkars mig, jeg har grått i hele nat
      poor me, I have cried all night
    • 1916, Barbra Ring, Under seil, page 14:
      hun er næsten tre aar ældre end jeg
      she is almost three years older than I am
    • 1917, Sigbjørn Obstfelder, “De røde dråber”, in Skrifter‎, volume I, page 161:
      Kald mig bare pige … Jeg er ikke andet jeg.
      Just call me a servant girl … I am nothing else.
  2. (rare) one, you; used generically when presenting a general principle from an individual's perspective.[2]
    Hvis jeg vil bli bedre, må jeg øve. ― If one wants to improve, one must practise.
Usage notes
  • Written with a lowercase initial except where ordinary capitalization rules require a capital, such as at the beginning of a sentence.
  • The object form is meg, which is also used reflexively. The possessive forms are min, mi, mitt and mine.
  • Both jeg and meg are accepted as predicative complements: det er jeg or det er meg (“it is me”). In cleft constructions, the form normally follows the pronoun's underlying grammatical role: det var jeg som ropte (“it was I who shouted”), but det var meg de ropte på (“it was me they called for”).[3]
  • After enn (“than”) and som (“as”), both forms are accepted when the comparison concerns the subject. Using jeg can clarify an otherwise ambiguous comparison.[4]
  • In conversational language, an unstressed repetition may occur at the end of a clause: Det vet jeg ikke, jeg. (“I don't know.”).
  • Literary exclamations may use the subject form, as in Å, jeg ulykkelige! (“Oh, unhappy me!”).
Derived terms
  • jeg-form (“first-person narration”)
  • jeg-forteller (“first-person narrator”)
  • jeg-litteratur (“first-person literature”)
  • jeg-roman (“first-person novel”)

Etymology 2

Nominalization of jeg (“I”, pronoun).

Compare the parallel nominalizations Norwegian Nynorsk eg, Danish jeg, Swedish jag, German Ich and Dutch ik (“self, ego”).

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /jæɪ̯/, [jæɪ̯]
  • Audio:(file)
  • Rhymes: -æɪ̯
  • Homophone: jei
  • Hyphenation: jeg

Noun

jeg n (definite singular jeget, indefinite plural jeg or jeger, definite plural jega or jegene)

  1. self; one's person, personality or individual identity.
    Hun følte at hun endelig kunne være sitt egentlige jeg. ― She felt that she could finally be her true self.
    ens annet jeg, ens andre jeg — one's alter ego; another side of one's personality, or a closely kindred person.
    På scenen fikk hun vise sitt andre jeg. ― On stage she could show her other self.
    ens bedre jeg — one's better self, or the moral side of one's personality.
    Hun appellerte til hans bedre jeg. ― She appealed to his better self.
    Synonyms: selv, ego
    • 1852, Henrik Ibsen, “Sancthansnatten”, in Efterladte Skrifter, volume I, published 1909, page 406:
      Hvilket af mine to Jeg’er har Ret?
      Which of my two selves is right?
    • 1867, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, page 165:
      Nu er jeg altsaa Ægypter till Forandring; / men Ægypter paa Grundlag af det gyntske jeg.
      Now, then, I am an Egyptian for a change; / but an Egyptian founded on the Gyntian self.
    • 1884, Henrik Ibsen, Vildanden‎, Act III:
      La' os slå en streg over nattens hændelser. Sligt afhænger jo ikke af mit bedre jeg.
      Let us draw a line under last night's events. Such things are not, after all, governed by my better self.
    • 1891, Arne Garborg, “Trætte Mænd”, in Skriftir i Samling‎, volume III, published 1909, page 160:
      Og med skaansom Lemfældighed sætter jeg de gamle, skjæve Støvler, der var blevne en Del af mit Jeg, op paa et Loft […]
      And with gentle care I put the old, misshapen boots, which had become part of my self, up in an attic […]
    • 1907, Bernt Lie, Mot Overmagt, page 196:
      hendes gode jeg hadde seiret over hendes daarlige
      her good self had triumphed over her bad one
    • 1988 January 23, Aftenposten, page 7:
      utilstrekkelighetsfølelsen er blitt mitt annet jeg
      the feeling of inadequacy has become my other self
  2. (philosophy) self, subject; the subject of consciousness, especially considered as a unity underlying changing experiences.
    Filosofen skilte mellom jeget og omverdenen. ― The philosopher distinguished between the self and the outside world.
    det rene jeg — the pure ego; consciousness considered apart from its contents.
    • 2025 July 22, Ulrik Malt, Knut Erik Tranøy, “jeg”, in Store norske leksikon‎:
      Hos Johann G. Fichte er jeg-et og dets erkjennelse av et ikke-jeg et grunnleggende filosofisk utgangspunkt.
      For Johann G. Fichte, the self and its cognition of a non-self constitute a fundamental philosophical starting point.
  3. (psychoanalysis) ego; the part of the personality that regulates instinctual impulses in relation to external reality.
    I Freuds teori må jeget forholde seg til både driftene og virkeligheten. ― In Freud's theory, the ego must deal with both instinctual drives and reality.
    Synonym: ego
    • 2025 July 22, Ulrik Malt, Knut Erik Tranøy, “jeg”, in Store norske leksikon‎:
      Ifølge psykoanalytisk teori er jeg-et den realitetsorienterte, regulerende personlighetsinstansen.
      According to psychoanalytic theory, the ego is the reality-oriented, regulating agency of the personality.
  4. (literature) A first-person narrator or lyric speaker.
    Jeget i diktet er ikke nødvendigvis forfatteren. ― The speaker in the poem is not necessarily the author.
    • 2026, Isalill Kolpus, Hvem brente John Savio?, page 128:
      jeg-et i diktet er en enkel sjel
      the speaker in the poem is a simple soul
Derived terms
  • jeg-bevissthet (“self-awareness”)
  • jeg-bok (“autobiographical book”)
  • jeg-forfatter (“autobiographical or confessional writer”)
  • jeg-følelse (“sense of self”)
  • overjeg (“superego”)
